newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks dogged by weak bonds.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks dogged by weak bonds.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks were dragged lower Thursday by a stiff sell-off in the bond market that pushed long-term interest rates to their highest level in a month.

At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was off 10.06 points at 6,412.88. In the broader market, declining issues led advances 12-10 on active volume of 285 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
But the smaller name stocks did better, with the Nasdaq Composite index up 2.36 to 1,299.38, and the American Stock Exchange index gaining 1.31 to 590.30.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond plunged 1-12/32, boosting its yield to 6.50 percent -- the highest since Nov. 8 -- from 6.40 percent at Wednesday's close.
While the weak bond market clearly hurt stocks, analysts noted that stocks actually held their ground fairly well.

"Part of the reason the bond market is getting beaten up is that the bond market has not had any kind of sell-off yet," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "The stock market market at least has had some sell-off."
Smaller stocks rose even as blue chips were falling. The divergence was consistent with recent sessions that have seen small capitalisation stocks eke out gains, while big name stocks fell.
Analysts said, however, that investors clearly remained cautious, even about shares in smaller companies.
"There certainly is something going on, and it's been going on for two weeks, with the small caps playing catch up," said Johnson.
"But one of the things you don't want to do is buy small caps when you're worried about the economy, and there still are worries about the economy and the market for 1997," he said.
With key employment and wage data due Friday, analysts said buyers were likely to remain sidelined in the bond market for the rest of the session.
"Up to now, Treasuries have just been magical," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "With Treasuries down there's little appetite to buy stocks."
Financial companies took the most direct hit from the jump in long-term interest rates.
Citicorp fell 2-1/2 to 103-3/8 and Chase Manhattan Corp. sank 2-1/4 to 88-3/8.
Among individual issues, sunglass maker Oakley Inc. fell 4-1/4 to 11-1/8 after saying that it expected its fourth quarter earnings would fall below analysts' estimates.
Pier 1 Imports Inc. gained 1-1/8 to 16. The company reported its same-store sales rose 16.3 percent in November.
Compaq Computer Corp. rose 2-1/8 to 83-7/8 after Deutsche Morgan Grenfell raised its fourth quarter and 1997 earnings estimates on the company.
